q: Why must a reversible reaction be carried out in a closed system for equilibrium to be reached?
options: So that no reactants or products can escape
So that a catalyst can be added
So that the forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction
So that heat can escape
explain: If a gas could escape, the reaction mixture could not be returned to the reactants and equilibrium would not be reached.

q: For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) at equilibrium, which statement is correct?
options: Both the forward and reverse reactions are still taking place
Only the forward reaction is taking place
Neither reaction is taking place
Only the reverse reaction is taking place
explain: Equilibrium is dynamic. Both reactions continue but at equal rates, so there is no overall change.

q: Which symbol equation represents the reaction in the Haber process?
options: 2N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 4NH₃(g)
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
N₂(g) + 2H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
N₂(g) + H₂(g) ⇌ NH₃(g)
explain: Only N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ has equal numbers of N atoms (2) and H atoms (6) on each side.

q: Which row correctly gives a raw material and its source for the Haber process?
options: Hydrogen | liquid air
Nitrogen | methane
Hydrogen | air
Nitrogen | air
explain: Nitrogen comes from the air. Hydrogen comes from methane (natural gas).

q: Which are the typical conditions used in the Haber process?
options: 25 °C, 200 atm, platinum catalyst
450 °C, 200 atm, vanadium(V) oxide catalyst
450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalyst
450 °C, 2 atm, iron catalyst
explain: The Haber process uses about 450 °C, 20 000 kPa (200 atm) and an iron catalyst.

q: Which are the typical conditions used for the conversion of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide in the Contact process?
options: 450 °C, 2 atm, vanadium(V) oxide catalyst
450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalyst
450 °C, 200 atm, vanadium(V) oxide catalyst
450 °C, 2 atm, iron catalyst
explain: The Contact process uses about 450 °C, 200 kPa (2 atm) and a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst.

q: Which equation shows the conversion of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide in the Contact process?
options: S(s) + O₂(g) ⇌ SO₂(g)
2SO₂(g) + 2O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)
SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ SO₃(g)
explain: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ has 2 S atoms and 6 O atoms on each side. The others are unbalanced or show a different reaction.

q: What are the sources of sulfur dioxide for the Contact process?
options: Neutralising sulfuric acid with ammonia
Cracking crude oil
Fractional distillation of liquid air
Burning sulfur or roasting sulfide ores in air
explain: Sulfur dioxide is made by burning sulfur in air or by roasting metal sulfide ores. Oxygen comes from the air.

q: The forward reaction in the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), is exothermic. What happens to the equilibrium yield of ammonia if the temperature is increased at constant pressure?
options: It increases, because the equilibrium shifts to the right
It increases, because the rate of reaction increases
It stays the same
It decreases, because the equilibrium shifts to the left
explain: Increasing the temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction, so the equilibrium shifts to the left and less ammonia is present.

q: Why does increasing the pressure increase the equilibrium yield of ammonia in N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
options: The reaction is exothermic, so high pressure favours it
There are fewer gas molecules on the right, so the equilibrium shifts to the right
High pressure acts as a catalyst
There are more gas molecules on the right, so the equilibrium shifts to the right
explain: There are 4 gas molecules on the left and 2 on the right. Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules.

q: The reaction H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) is at equilibrium. What is the effect of increasing the pressure at constant temperature?
options: The position of equilibrium does not change, as there are equal numbers of gas molecules on both sides
The reaction stops
The equilibrium shifts to the left
The equilibrium shifts to the right
explain: There are 2 gas molecules on each side, so pressure does not favour either direction.

q: The equilibrium 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g) has NO₂ as a brown gas and N₂O₄ as a colourless gas. The forward reaction is exothermic. A sealed tube of the equilibrium mixture is cooled. What is observed?
options: The mixture becomes paler as the equilibrium shifts to the right
The colour does not change
The mixture becomes paler as the equilibrium shifts to the left
The mixture becomes darker brown as the equilibrium shifts to the left
explain: Cooling favours the exothermic forward reaction, so more colourless N₂O₄ forms and the brown colour fades.

q: In the Haber process, ammonia is removed as it forms. What is the effect on the position of equilibrium?
options: It shifts to the right, so more ammonia is formed
The reaction can no longer take place
It does not change
It shifts to the left, so less ammonia is formed
explain: Removing a product lowers its concentration, so the system makes more of it to restore equilibrium.

q: What is the effect of the iron catalyst on the Haber process?
options: It shifts the equilibrium to the left
It shifts the equilibrium to the right
It does not change the position of equilibrium but equilibrium is reached faster
Equilibrium is never reached
explain: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but the position is unchanged.

q: Why is a temperature of 450 °C used in the Haber process rather than a much lower temperature?
options: A lower temperature would decrease the rate and also decrease the yield
A lower temperature would give too slow a rate, so 450 °C is a compromise between rate and yield
450 °C gives the highest possible yield of ammonia
A lower temperature would increase the rate but decrease the yield
explain: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature gives a higher yield but too slow a rate. 450 °C gives an acceptable rate and yield.

q: Why is a pressure much higher than 200 atm not used in the Haber process?
options: Higher pressure would decrease the equilibrium yield of ammonia
Higher pressure would decrease the rate of reaction
The equipment would be very expensive to build and run, and more dangerous
The iron catalyst stops working above 200 atm
explain: Higher pressure increases the yield but needs stronger, more costly equipment and creates a greater safety risk, so 200 atm is a compromise.

q: Why is the Contact process carried out at only about 2 atm?
options: Vanadium(V) oxide does not work above 2 atm
Higher pressure would shift the equilibrium to the left
Sulfur dioxide would become a solid at higher pressure
The yield of sulfur trioxide is already high, so higher pressure would add cost for little gain
explain: The conversion of SO₂ to SO₃ is high at about 2 atm and 450 °C. High-pressure equipment would add cost and safety risk with little extra yield.

q: The forward reaction in the Contact process is exothermic. Why is a temperature of 450 °C used instead of 100 °C?
options: At 100 °C the vanadium(V) oxide catalyst would be used up
At 100 °C the yield of sulfur trioxide would be lower
At 100 °C the rate would be too slow, even though the equilibrium yield would be higher
At 450 °C the equilibrium yield is the highest possible
explain: Lower temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction but the rate becomes too slow. 450 °C is a compromise.

q: What is the purpose of the vanadium(V) oxide catalyst in the Contact process?
options: To increase the rate at which equilibrium is reached
To react permanently with oxygen
To increase the equilibrium yield of sulfur trioxide
To supply the sulfur dioxide
explain: The catalyst makes the reaction faster but does not change the position of equilibrium.

q: In the Haber process the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled to the reactor. What is the reason?
options: The gases must be cooled before they are used
The reaction cannot start without recycled gases
The recycled gases act as a catalyst
Only part of the mixture reacts on each pass, and recycling avoids wasting the reactants
explain: At equilibrium the mixture still contains much unreacted gas, so recycling it makes use of all the reactants and saves money.

q: Which row correctly describes the Haber process?
options: Contact | nitrogen from air, hydrogen from methane | vanadium(V) oxide
Haber | nitrogen from air, hydrogen from methane | iron
Contact | sulfur dioxide from burning sulfur, oxygen from air | iron
Haber | nitrogen from air, hydrogen from methane | vanadium(V) oxide
explain: The Haber process uses nitrogen from air and hydrogen from methane with an iron catalyst. The Contact process uses vanadium(V) oxide and different raw materials.

q: For a reversible reaction the forward reaction is endothermic. Which change increases the yield of products at equilibrium?
options: Increasing the temperature
Decreasing the temperature
Adding a catalyst and decreasing the temperature
Adding a catalyst
explain: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, so the equilibrium shifts towards the products. A catalyst does not change the position.

q: A reversible reaction starts with only reactants and reaches equilibrium in a closed system. Which statement about the rates is correct?
options: The reverse rate is always greater than the forward rate
The forward rate increases until it is zero
The forward rate decreases and the reverse rate increases until they are equal
The rates stay different but the concentrations stop changing
explain: The forward rate falls as reactants are used, and the reverse rate rises as products build up. At equilibrium they are equal.

q: In the Haber process N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), what is the maximum amount of ammonia that could be made from 3.0 mol of hydrogen with excess nitrogen if the reaction went to completion?
options: 2.0 mol
1.5 mol
3.0 mol
6.0 mol
explain: The mole ratio H₂ : NH₃ is 3 : 2, so 3.0 mol of H₂ gives 3.0 × 2/3 = 2.0 mol of NH₃.

q: What is the name of the compound with formula Fe₂O₃?
options: Iron(VI) oxide
Iron(V) oxide
Iron(II) oxide
Iron(III) oxide
explain: Two Fe ions balance three O²⁻ ions (total 6−), so each iron ion is 3+. The Roman numeral III shows the oxidation number of iron.

q: What is the formula of copper(I) oxide?
options: CuO₂
Cu₂O₃
CuO
Cu₂O
explain: Copper(I) has an oxidation number of +1, so two Cu⁺ ions are needed to balance one O²⁻ ion.

q: Which compound contains iron in the +2 oxidation state?
options: FeCl₃
Fe₂O₃
Fe₂(SO₄)₃
FeCl₂
explain: In FeCl₂ two Cl⁻ ions balance one Fe²⁺. The other compounds contain iron(III).

q: What does the (IV) mean in the name manganese(IV) oxide?
options: There are four manganese atoms in the formula
There are four oxygen atoms in the formula
Manganese is in Group IV of the Periodic Table
The oxidation number of manganese is +4
explain: The Roman numeral gives the oxidation number of the metal. Manganese(IV) oxide is MnO₂.

q: Which statement describes a redox reaction?
options: Only oxidation takes place
A solution changes from acidic to neutral
Oxidation and reduction take place at the same time
A solid dissolves in water
explain: Redox means reduction and oxidation together. One substance is oxidised while another is reduced.

q: Which is the definition of oxidation in terms of oxygen?
options: Loss of oxygen
Gain of water
Loss of mass
Gain of oxygen
explain: A substance is oxidised when it gains oxygen, and reduced when it loses oxygen.
